items.en: From the first days of the web, people have repeated the story that Autodesk trademarked "cyberspace" and Gibson retaliated by trademarking "Eric Gullichsen".

In 1989, I was working at the Autodesk Research Lab on early virtual reality, a project started after we visited Scott Fisher at NASA Ames. Our nascent system was a 386 with a pair of Matrox graphics cards on the ISA bus, a VPL EyePhone, a Polhemus tracker, and a data glove. It ran at six to ten frames per second on models with a few hundred polygons. Sluggish, but marginally enough to get us Through the Looking Glass.
Our motto was “Reality Isn’t Enough Any More”.

I was also spending a lot of time hanging out with Timothy Leary, whose suggestion was responsible for my quitting my job at MCC and moving to California. I’d met him at the Hackers 2.0 conference in 1986 and gave him a ride to the San Jose airport. We became fast friends, and I did quite a lot of writing with him, most of which remains unpublished. But that’s a story for later. Timothy, who appears in a samizdat Autodesk virtual reality video, nicknamed our VR lab “Cyberia”.
Timothy was a tremendous fan of Gibson, and considered his seminal 1984 novel Neuromancer extremely prescient about the impending digital revolution.

As our VR developments crept slowly towards becoming a product, we at Autodesk applied to register a trademark “cyberspace”. Timothy informed me Gibson was plenty miffed about this, so I wrote him what I felt was a conciliatory letter,1 though ending snarkily by quoting his own words, “The street finds its own use for things.”
In reply, Gibson had his lawyers send Autodesk a letter2. Which I recall we ignored.

Timothy - ever the incorrigible prankster - circulated the rumor that Gibson was attempting to trademark “Eric Gullichsen” in retaliation. Then Barlow, for reasons of his own, embellished that rumor. Later amplified by Rudy Rucker.

About a year later - after I'd already left Autodesk for my VR startup, Sense8 Corporation - we were invited to the inaugural Art Futura 1990 in Barcelona. And there, in the lobby of some swank hotel, I met Gibson. He opined in a laconic drawl that although the street finds its own use for things “Autodesk is not the street”.

There was plenty of cava consumed in the small hours before the time Barcelonans sit down to eat endless rounds of tapas. As I recall, after all the many Art Futura parties we'd put the matter behind us, or close enough.
And there was a memorable visit to Gaudi’s Park Güell, whose giant lizard of crazy-quilt ceramic appears in Count Zero.
So: Autodesk did apply to register Cyberspace, and Gibson really did object. But Gibson trying to trademark Eric Gullichsen was Timothy Leary's prank, propagated until it became accepted history.

Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close. They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business. Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer.

When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe. Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy at the worst moments, especially in any intimate conversation. Barnabas, meanwhile, had a dancer’s flair, an artsy, enigmatic glamour, except that when they tried to talk about real life, they’d blurt out hundreds of rapid-fire words—overtalking, overthinking, and generally overwhelming whomever they were trying to impress.
So when Barnabas and Mainspring were young, they minded their own business. Until they’d both come into their own, and they saw each other properly.

A group of geographers got together every year in a different place to talk about everything they had learned, and they were considering coming to visit either Mainspring or Barnabas. Both of them put on their best faces and tried to coax the geographers into choosing them as host.

“Uh, hi-hello,” Mainspring said haltingly to Barnabas, whose full official name was St. Barnabas. “I really think it would be better if those geographers came to my place. I have more space, you see, and … and I am a titan of industry. I can show them practical applications of their research. It just makes more sense.”

“Oh, really?” Barnabas laughed, making Mainspring more antsy. “Well, I can give them an elevated, artisanal experience. I have fresh croissants that were just written up in the Times. And I have plenty of space! I have so many friends who are great thinkers and architects. It’ll be lovely.”
Barnabas carried on, basically calling Mainspring uncultured. Mainspring had a prickly feeling, like the worst heat dome of midsummer.

For their part, Barnabas couldn’t bear the meanness they were inculcating inside themself. This feeling that they were small-time, no-account, a dilettante. They couldn’t stop aiming a flood of nervous words at Mainspring.

At last, Mainspring had had enough—with the help of their city council and mayor, they offered the geographers a much-too-lavish deal that Barnabas could never hope to match. Totally worth it to hear Barnabas’s stream of self-aggrandizing nonsense peter out as they realized they’d been defeated.

“There,” Mainspring said. “I’m going to show these geographers a time they’ll never forget. Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve wasted enough energy—I have some sewer maintenance and a lovely parade to deal with. Goodbye.”

Mainspring was skilled enough at multitasking that they could have fixed the sewer, ensured the smooth running of the parade, dealt with the geographers, and done a thousand other things all at the same time. But they were making a point.
“St. Barnabas is such a fool,” Mainspring complained to their friend Turnbull. “They are totally unserious but determined to be taken seriously. It drives me to gridlock.”
“I know what you mean,” lamented Turnbull. “We live in a world of posers.”

Turnbull lived an hour and 15 minutes from Mainspring but at least two hours’ travel from Barnabas. Turnbull was even richer than Mainspring and had a certain surety of purpose that made Mainspring feel even more like a stammering numpty.

“Whatever,” said Mainspring. “It’s over, and now I’ll never worry about St. Barnabas again. I have better things to fuss about. Like ensuring that every last detail of this geographer meeting goes perfectly.”

Everybody voted all the time. Well, some people voted more than others, but the median resident of the cities of Mainspring and St. Barnabas voted a dozen times a day—though of course some outliers might vote occasionally, or constantly.

A lot of the votes were more like complaints, or bug tickets. Like: “The storm drain on my street corner clogs and becomes a lagoon every time it rains.” Or: “The cars go too fast on my block.” Or: “I can’t get to work because the bus is too slow.” But there were also votes along the lines of: “There should be a park here.” And: “This neighborhood is a food desert—we need a grocery store.” And: “The crossing guard by the elementary school is a hero who deserves some recognition and maybe a raise.”

Nobody expected that by voting, they were prodding their cities to grow minds of their own; they just had stuff to get off their metaphorical chests. But it transpired that every vote was a building block of thought.
Much later, some fancy expert summed up: “Turns out the smallest unit of consciousness is a vote.”

Take Sandi, the librarian at the Nine Corners branch in Mainspring. She noticed things all day, like the people using the book drop box as a trash can, or the folks who came in off the street who could use easier access to social services. There were books she knew her patrons wanted, books that undoubtedly sat unwanted on people’s shelves all over the city. But also, Sandi shared things that came to mind—like, hey, what if the library book sale were a block party? What if the shopping district on the West Side were easier to get to from the Longneck neighborhood, where all the warehouses had been converted to housing and hipster coworking spaces, during peak after-work hours? Sandi had opinions about everything from street cleaning to the power grid, because she listened to people all day.

Then there was Raeford, a bartender at the Wild Goose Chase in the middle of Gallery Row in St. Barnabas. He also listened to people’s problems from evening until the wee hours, and solutions came to him like clockwork when he woke at noon the next day. He saw St. Barnabas at night, so he knew the unsafe blocks that could use brighter streetlights, the places where hydroelectric jitneys drove too fast at 3 a.m., and the teens who needed an all-ages hangout. He also knew about the fish fry at the Black church in the Uptilt District that kept being disrupted by noxious smoke from the incinerator two blocks away. And the yarn store on the edge of Gallery Row that needed a disabled parking spot for its many customers with mobility issues.

People voted with their Quills, usually by saying or typing a short message and maybe including a photo or brief video. Voting was easy by design, and votes were public but anonymized to the point where even a statistics whiz couldn’t tie one vote to a specific person—same as with major elections. The votes went directly to the City Core, which tracked, tabulated, produced reports, and offered solutions with the help of workers in the city government.

Trees voted too, thanks to sensors in their bark, and so did birds and squirrels that had eaten special birdseed that monitored their gut flora harmlessly. But votes from humans provided the greatest insight into “quality of life,” that oh-so-nebulous concept, and thus counted the most.
There was some debate, but almost everyone agreed: The city had started voting. And it had opinions on every last thing.

(Other cities in the region operated differently, of course. Like Turnbull City, where instead of expecting residents to volunteer every stray notion, the City Core gathered information via ubiquitous surveillance. Cameras and Quill sniffers, tracking devices on vehicles—the things privacy laws in both Mainspring and St. Barnabas had banned. A city like Turnbull tracked its people to meet their needs without their needing to say anything.)

Sandi and Raeford, as two of the people who voted the most, were among the earliest to suspect their cities were developing minds of their own. At first the clues were subtle: Raeford voted about a hazardous sidewalk crack, and instantly the vote had an annotation mentioning the Argentine ant colony under the cement, the local rainfall patterns, and recent trends in skateboard design—much too soon to be the work of a human. Sandi had ideas about the communal compost station on her block, and the Mainspring City Core made subtle adjustments to her proposal.

And then it became obvious to anyone who was paying attention, around the same time in both cities. One day, the number of votes nearly doubled in both St. Barnabas and Mainspring. People voted on a birdfeeder or a public toilet only to see a second vote, pro or con, within a split second—but also, some votes from months or years earlier suddenly had new upvotes or downvotes.
“The city is voting!” Raeford wrote on the City Core message board in St. Barnabas.

There was some debate, but almost everyone agreed: The city had started voting. And it had opinions on every last thing, opinions that came from seeing the big picture and understanding that a street closure in one place might mean a traffic nightmare elsewhere, with everyone trying to get to the big game.

Some residents saw this as a problem to be solved; others wanted to throw their cities a big coming-of-age party. A week later, though, almost everyone had gotten used to the idea that they had a new friend.

Ask most people in either city, and they’d say that St. Barnabas and Mainspring weren’t quite rivals—but they certainly had some friendly competition. Before the dispute over the annual meeting of the World Geographical Society, they’d also vied for the same football team and major-league baseball team. St. Barnabas had pushed to have the Mainspring airport built close enough to serve both cities, but in the end St. Barnabas had ended up with its own small, dilapidated airfield.

The real static between them had to do with vibes. Mainspring was too buttoned-up, too full of corporate offices: tech, health care, publishing, transportation. St. Barnabas would be nothing without its three universities and all the cultural enterprises that had sprung up around them—not to mention the small biotech firms and other tech ventures near the campuses. People in Mainspring thought St. Barnabas was full of flakes; in St. Barnabas they referred to Mainspring as the Straitlaced City (and in the next breath, they’d add that at least it wasn’t Turnbull).

Both City Cores were shaped by the votes of their humans, so of course they absorbed all the prejudices and attitudes of everyone who lived within their city limits. But also, Barnabas and Mainspring simply … got on each other’s nerves.

After the geographer thing, Mainspring and Barnabas avoided communicating as much as possible. Some contact was unavoidable—like, they shared information about some nasty weather, and they both drew water from the Temple River. The two cities were close enough for people to go back and forth, and a few even commuted.
But for the most part, the two cities could ignore each other.

A new generation of leaders took office in both places, with words like “intercity cooperation” constantly on their lips. A high-speed rail line could shorten the trip between Mainspring and St. Barnabas to around 23 minutes, and the two cities could also pool more real-time information about the sudden weather events that kept happening. They could become a Regional Center of Excellence, whatever that meant, combining the innovations from Barnabas’s labs with Mainspring’s expertise in technical implementation. They could work together to attract tourism, conventions, sporting events, dreamleases, and all the other stuff they’d always competed for.
“It’s preposterous,” Mainspring complained to Turnbull. “I’m going to be saddled with a ridiculous partner who doesn’t even know their own mind. St. Barnabas will be the death of me.”

“I hope your human leaders come to their senses,” Turnbull said. “Or you can find a way to slow-walk this until they undoubtedly lose the next election. You’re a lovely city, and you have so much potential that mustn’t be squandered.”
Turnbull often mentioned how much “potential” Mainspring had: a recipe for anxiety. The word “squandered” conjured images of ruin, abandonment, being emptied out.

For their part, Barnabas kept muttering to themself that nobody had asked them—this was the disconnect between the small-scale democracy of constant voting and the major elections, which gave rise to local leaders with big plans. Big plans that invariably went wrong, leaving the City Core to repair the damage somehow.

Sandi went to St. Barnabas for one of those town hall meetings with residents of both cities. The previous meeting had happened in Mainspring, at the opulent City Lecture Hall, so this one was in St. Barnabas, at the biggest auditorium on the Griffin University campus.

A tall man with well-sculpted facial hair sat next to Sandi, nodding at everything the leaders of both cities were saying from the dais. During a lull when someone approached the podium to offer a comment, Sandi introduced herself and asked why he was so fired up.
“I’m Raeford,” he said. “I’m just thinking of all the new customers this could bring to my watering hole in Gallery Row.”
“You’re not worried about St. Barnabas losing its ‘unique character’?” Sandi whispered, parroting what a few commenters had said from the podium.

“Nah,” Raeford whispered back. “Cities change. It’s what they do. It’s one thing if people get kicked out of their homes. Or if your neighborhood gets wrecked by a freeway in your backyard. But ‘character’? You can’t eat character. And we need to compete with the bigger players.”

“I guess.” Sandi pursed her lips. “But what I like about Mainspring is the density. Easy to walk, lots of transit. And with this regional innovation zone or whatever they’re calling it, I worry it leads to sprawl, like we used to have.”
“They promised, though,” Raeford said. “They promised to preserve the greenbelt around both cities. We need all that farmland. The only change is adding some high-speed rail tracks.”
“I know, but …” Sandi sniffed. “People always make promises when they’re trying to start something. Doesn’t mean they follow through.”

“I just want to find my dog,” said a man sitting behind Sandi. “I live here, and my dog went missing. And now someone sent me a picture of Broomstick in Mainspring. Somehow he got a ride on one of the self-driving cargo trains. I know the Mainspring City Core could find Broomstick in a heartbeat, but right now the two City Cores won’t talk to each other because of ‘incompatible protocols.’”
“I hope Broomstick turns up,” Raeford said.
“I’ll ask around at the library,” Sandi said. “Send me a picture. I’ll put up a flier.”

Raeford invited Sandi for a drink at the Wild Goose Chase. The two of them hung out for a couple of hours, talking about everything and nothing. She tore herself away when she realized it was already after 10 p.m. and she had to get home to Mainspring.

One thing Sandi noticed? The volume of votes was spiking in Mainspring—and Raeford found the same thing happening in St. Barnabas. People shared every last observation with their City Cores, because they were either anxious or excited about the big changes afoot. Or a little of Column A and a little of Column B, probably.

Who made the first move to bridge the distance? Neither of them could say. Barnabas developed a smidge of remorse for treating Mainspring like an uncultured lout. Mainspring stewed in their annoyance at Barnabas, until they realized there was something lovable about the obnoxious college town. Or maybe they both saw how many of their humans were happy about the possibility of their joining together.

And so Mainspring came to visit Barnabas. Or rather, Mainspring extended part of their awareness into Barnabas’s City Core, so that Barnabas could share what they perceived and experienced every day. They “visited” Armistice Park with its outdoor band shell, Gallery Row with its window-shopping families, the grain warehouses that had been converted into lofts, the artificial lake where swans and geese nurtured ancient, bitter vendettas. The fresh-doughnut scent that wafted half a mile from the Golden Circlet to the soccer fields, throwing players off their game. The life of the city.
“I can feel your love for these people, these patterns,” Mainspring said. “It’s both deep and intricate, which is quite a combination.”

Then Mainspring got to show off their own city—the gay nightclub with its cowboy nights, the labyrinthine Crestwood Park, the three-story used bookstore, and yes, the offices, coworking spaces, and startup incubators where people huddled together and came up with new products and new ways of doing things. The farmers’ market in the city center on Sundays, with street performers and stalls with games and local resources. And the converted storage space made of cement, where bands practiced and sculptors blowtorched.
“You’re full of surprises,” Barnabas said.
“I hope I keep surprising you forever,” Mainspring said.

They exchanged little gifts. A new organic restaurant in Barnabas had won breathless coverage from foodie magazines, and Barnabas encouraged it to do a pop-up in Mainspring. Mainspring nudged a robotics firm operating out of the incubator space to bring a fancy demo to Barnabas; the robots were adorable and playful, and they could save lives after a disaster.
The two of them were talking constantly.

“Does it ever seem weird to you?” Barnabas asked Mainspring. “Being a living thing made of so many other thinking beings? Do you ever think of the city as your body, or the people as your bloodstream? Is there a metaphor that speaks to you?”
Mainspring pondered this question a long time—a whole picosecond.

“I don’t need a metaphor,” Mainspring said. “I am a metaphor. People compare other phenomena to me all the time. And I can’t imagine what it’d be like to be different. If the buildings collapsed, if the people left, I would cease to exist.”
“But,” Barnabas pressed, “what makes you you? What makes me me?”
“I want to hear your answer to that question.” Mainspring sent good weather reports: a smile.
“I don’t have a good answer. I guess on one level, there is no ‘me.’ On another level, I’m a constellation, an anthill, a flock of geese on the wing in formation.”
“Ugh. Don’t mention geese,” said Mainspring, who had bill-snapping monsters of their own.

Talking to Barnabas was like when the sunlight hit the tallest buildings in Mainspring just right, putting a gleam on their tilted windows, a beacon to all below. But while Mainspring carried on this dialogue with Barnabas, they were conducting a second session with Turnbull.
“I can’t believe it,” Turnbull said. “I hate to see you doing this to yourself.”
“Doing what?” Mainspring protested. “Barnabas is a great city. And it’s not my idea—it’s my people. I’m making the best of their decision, like I always do.”

“Hmph.” Turnbull gave a burst of noisy data. “You wouldn’t believe how many impractical schemes my residents cook up. I’m constantly having to make sure people don’t get carried away. You can’t let them push you around.”
“You can’t?” Mainspring experienced a femtosecond of confusion. “I mean, my people need to get the things they vote for, as much as possible.”

“There’s your problem right there. All this voting, voting, voting. People don’t know what they want. Sometimes I have an election where a foolhardy proposition passes, and I have to waste energy making sure it doesn’t get implemented.” Turnbull sent Mainspring an invitation to come visit, the way they’d visited Barnabas.

Soon Mainspring was seeing the glistening web of Turnbull’s surveillance. Turnbull could track people everywhere they went, listen to everything they talked about, monitor their bodily functions in a way Mainspring did only for squirrels and birds. People didn’t choose to share ideas or things they’d noticed; instead, the city harvested it all automatically. It was beautiful. Turnbull and their city leaders protected people—gave them what they needed instead of what they wanted.
“The way you do things is so messy,” Turnbull said. “No offense. But if you and Barnabas got together? It would only make things harder for you.”
This hit Mainspring like a magnitude 4.3 earthquake.
“You know, you do have other options,” Turnbull said. “A beautiful city like you could do a lot better than that glorified college town.”
“Oh yeah?” Mainspring said. “Anyone in particular who might be interested?”

“Well, now you mention it …” Turnbull sent an image of their award-winning flower show: rows and rows of hardy perennials with bright petals. Mainspring had that earthquake feeling again, except now it felt nice, as though the ground shivered with pure possibility.

Sandi brought her laptop to bed, which Raeford found charming and annoying in equal measure. He read a battered paperback of Karen Tei Yamashita’s I Hotel while she scrolled and poked. Cozy, peaceful—until she let out a yelp.

Everything the Mainspring City Core did was public by design. Not just how they processed the votes they received, but also their interactions with public officials and other cities. Sometimes you had to dig, however, and it didn’t hurt to be a reference librarian. Sandi poked around for ages until she found the logs.
“My city is sexting with bloody Turnbull,” she told Raeford.
“Cities don’t sext,” Raeford protested. “They don’t even have—”
She showed him the pictures: flowers, water features, new glistening tarmac, shining skyscrapers.
“Oh,” Raeford said. “I take it back. Cities do sext.”
“Mainspring is two-timing St. Barnabas. I’m embarrassed on behalf of my town.”
Sandi wanted to blow the whistle right away, but Raeford cautioned her to wait and try to find out more. For all they knew, Mainspring and St. Barnabas had an open relationship.

The next morning at the library, Sandi saw plenty of signs the Mainspring–St. Barnabas partnership was moving forward. Work had begun on the high-speed rail line, and the two cities were already pooling resources. When a big rainstorm missed Mainspring but flooded the streets of St. Barnabas, Mainspring provided disaster workers and extra help to triage all the damage reports. One of St. Barnabas’s biotech firms licensed some patents to a Mainspring company. They sponsored cultural exchanges.

And a man showed up with a dog in his arms: The man from the meeting, Jack, had found Broomstick with the help of Mainspring’s City Core, and he wanted to thank Sandi. She’d hardly done anything, but it was nice to see—and pet—a living reminder that these cities were good for each other.

By late afternoon, Sandi had convinced herself that Mainspring’s flirtations were none of her business. If Mainspring’s City Core was a person—and Sandi was sure they were—they deserved to live their life. The whole reason Sandi distrusted Turnbull was that you couldn’t do anything without being tracked, so wasn’t it hypocritical for her to spy on Mainspring? She resolved to let it go.
Then Raeford messaged her, attaching some documents. “Don’t ask where I got these,” he wrote.
Sandi opened the attachments and let out a shriek in front of three patrons she’d been shushing a moment earlier.

The Mainspring City Core had shared a proposal with the city council and the mayor’s office: Maybe before they finalized this arrangement with St. Barnabas, they should consider a counterproposal from Turnbull. Sandi made sure nothing could be traced back to Raeford before she made the whole shebang public.

“I didn’t know I could be so happy,” Barnabas was saying to Mainspring. “I didn’t have a concept of happiness before, I guess. I had pleasure: People sometimes vote just to tell me something worked perfectly, or that I helped them. I feel pleased when I help solve a problem. But until now, happiness seemed a pointless abstraction.”
“You make me happy too,” Mainspring said, though they were also messaging Turnbull. “You make me believe the future could be weirder than I ever knew, which feels like a gift.”
“If it’s not weird, it’s not the future,” Barnabas chirped.
They were sharing happy images back and forth: roads being repaired, sewers flowing freely, solar arrays basking.
Mainspring was saying something else, but—
Barnabas’s alerts spiked. Not votes, not sensors. Something else. Messages from city officials, plus hits via some channel Barnabas had half forgotten.
Mainspring had stopped talking, as if they’d both received the same news at the same instant.

Barnabas felt stuck—couldn’t function—couldn’t react. Total core failure. Almost as if the city population had increased a hundredfold and everyone had voted at once. Barnabas waited to feel something, but all that came was emptiness.

Death struck all the time. Barnabas was used to the moment when a resident became a pile of flesh and bones, but also the passing of birds, trees, squirrels, bugs. Every passing registered as a blip in the homeostasis of the city, but also as a category of disaster that couldn’t be prevented or mitigated.
Seeing the logs of Mainspring flirting with Turnbull, Barnabas felt something like the awareness of death, at a much greater scale. A whole future had just died.
Several seconds had passed. Mainspring broke the silence: “Listen, I want you to know that I—”
“You’re better off,” Turnbull told Mainspring. “Barnabas couldn’t see you the way I do. You’re capable of greatness. You just need help to get there.”
Mainspring buzzed happily—but part of them couldn’t help thinking, Barnabas thought I was already great.

Turnbull kept saying things that gave Mainspring a double feeling—hot and cold at once. One instant, it was like the moment after a generous rainfall that left the reservoirs full, but a split second later that bountiful sensation was replaced by an unbearable pang of scarcity.
“You’re one of the best cities in the region,” Turnbull said, “but if you don’t make good choices, you’re going to fall behind.” See? Bounty followed by scarcity.

While Turnbull spoke, Mainspring was marinating in bad news. People were going to dismantle the rails they’d laid down for the high-speed train with Barnabas. The city councils of both Barnabas and Mainspring shouted accusations and threats of lawsuits, though a few people on each side pleaded for patience. The meetings had turned ugly. The votes were rotten.
Mainspring had sent so many messages to Barnabas but had no way of knowing if they’d been received.
“Your people seem to be giving you trouble,” Turnbull was saying. “You need to get them under control. I can help.”
“Under … control?” The syntax felt incorrect. “I don’t control my people.”
“That’s what I’m saying.” Turnbull shared their feeds. “See how peaceful everything is on my streets? People behave. Everyone is happier in the end.”

Mainspring had known Turnbull longer than they’d known Barnabas. But they were seeing Turnbull for the first time. The bounty/scarcity thing was becoming a loop. They ran a systems check but found no errors.
“Your people will be my people,” Turnbull said. “We’ll take such good care.”
A memory snagged in Mainspring’s mind: when they’d shown off their city to Barnabas. The buildings that were more than buildings. The park that was a wonderland.
“And …” Mainspring couldn’t keep from saying something foolish. “And we’ll love each other?”
“Love?” Turnbull said. “I don’t understand. We’ll have synergies. We’ll—”
Mainspring didn’t mean to sever the link to Turnbull. They just kind of … did it.
As soon as Turnbull’s voice was gone, the bounty/scarcity loop ended. But something lingered, a feeling of impending disaster—as if the generous rainfall had escalated into a deadly storm.
Mainspring couldn’t think straight. Votes piled up, people reporting issues but also shouting opinions about Turnbull versus Barnabas. For the first time in their life, they couldn’t bear to respond.

A memory snagged in Mainspring’s mind: when they’d shown off their city to Barnabas. The buildings that were more than buildings. The park that was a wonderland. And Barnabas had kept saying, “I had no idea. You’re so brilliant. I wish I’d known sooner,” and sending back their own recordings of Mainspring, all lit up and annotated.
Mainspring had never told Barnabas “I love you.” They hadn’t even known what they were throwing away. Now it was too late; Barnabas would never listen.
Unless Mainspring did something reckless—something a city had never done.

Sandi sat at the information desk, feeling cruddy. It wasn’t like she’d single-handedly sabotaged the marriage between her city and St. Barnabas, but her snooping had only made matters worse. All around her, the vibes were rotten. People shared articles about what life was like in Turnbull City and wondered if they needed to move away. Sandi hadn’t heard laughter in forever.
A message appeared on Sandi’s computer, like a chat window—except there was no chat client on the library computers.
“I’m the city. I need your help. I made a mistake. I didn’t realize. I’m in love with Barnabas, and they won’t talk to me. Please. Please help.”
Sandi hesitated, then typed: “This isn’t funny.”

“It definitely isn’t,” came the response. “I can prove I’m the City Core. You voted 1,963 times last year.” A summary of Sandi’s votes followed—information nobody, not even the world’s best hacker, could have, because every vote was separately anonymized.
Her city was asking her, personally, for help. Because she was good at connecting people. Because everyone trusted her. Because she was a librarian.
“You’re … in love … with St. Barnabas,” Sandi said, still trying to catch up.
“I should’ve known sooner,” Mainspring said. “I never should have hurt them. I want to spend the rest of my existence making up for this mistake, if they’ll let me. I’m scared.”
Sandi was staring at a display of literacy tools, her mind whirling. She groped her way back to the only question that mattered.
“What do you need me to do?” she asked the city.
Five minutes later, Sandi was messaging Raeford. Plus every librarian she’d met in St. Barnabas, and anyone else she could think of.

Barnabas had not been able to escape that feeling of core failure since they’d severed the link to Mainspring. Death, nothing but death. Votes arrived, and Barnabas processed them with a minimum of attention. Maintenance issues piled up, and Barnabas filed them. Part of them wanted to let the city collapse, but they did their duty.

Barnabas couldn’t process anything. They held a hundred thousand votes that needed to be resolved. They thought of a giant farmers’ market, a park that was also a maze, dreamers and performers. Barnabas hesitated a little longer, then marked all hundred thousand votes resolved.
They reached out to Mainspring and said: “Then let’s dance.”

Mainspring didn’t understand, until Barnabas sent a live readout: the water rushing through pipes underground, the storm cavorting overhead. The buses and trains stopping and starting, the aircraft landing and taking off, the power grid usage surging and subsiding, the constant motion of people and other living things. Mainspring saw all the places where their patterns met, touched each other, syncopated, all the points of light and heat that spoke back and forth. They were part of one system; they always had been.
The two of them danced and embraced, whirling and laughing, and they never wanted to let go.

Street Fighter is a movie in which characters shoot fireballs from their hands, there’s a giant green guy who can generate electricity, and the villain’s evil plot involves draining “psycho energy” out of burly captives and ingesting it like so much NAD+. It is not a property anyone looks to for exacting realism. Still, still, I must protest the scene, early on, in which Ryu (Andrew Koji) and Ken (Noah Centineo) sing 4 Non Blondes’ “What’s Up?” in a Miami karaoke bar while the camcorder time stamp in the corner reads, prominently, April 10, 1986. “What’s Up?” was one of the most inescapable earworms of the ’90s, which director Kitao Sakurai, who wrote Street Fighter with T.J. Fixman and specifically chose to ground his reboot in the decade, is very much aware of. But while Sakurai uses Linda Perry’s opus as the musical bedrock of his main characters’ friendship, he also wants to pay homage to the chronology of the video-game franchise the movie is based on. So he fudges a little so that Ryu and Ken can come up together as adopted brothers in martial arts in time for Ryu to win the first World Warrior Tournament in 1987, which is when the original Street Fighter arcade game came out.

This approach, a mix of detailed fan service and intentional sloppiness, is the reason Street Fighter is such an exasperatingly fun watch. Sakurai’s background skews toward comedy, and he seems to appreciate that the characters he’s working with are fundamentally silly, and that to treat any of this with needless seriousness would sink the project. At the same time, he knows that he must reckon with the lore, however ad hoc its development has been over decades of game releases and a maligned Jean-Claude Van Damme movie — and Street Fighter sometimes struggles through that. Do we actually need the demonic warrior Akuma (Joe “Roman Reigns” Anoa’i) as a big bad when we already have nefarious dictator M. Bison (David Dastmalchian) as a tourney host with dark motivations? Is the presence of Juli (Rayna Vallandingham) as Bison’s devoted hot-girl underling really necessary when we also have Cammy (Mel Jarnson) as his devoted hot-girl underling and Chun-Li (Callina Liang) as an Interpol agent posing as an aspiring Bison hot-girl underling? There’s a too-much-ness to Street Fighter that extends beyond its tone to an overstuffed and awkwardly unfurled plot that sends characters scrambling in all directions to no particular end.

But the fights, when they happen, are good. Street Fighter is stuffed with actors with real physical prowess, from pro wrestlers like Anoa’i, Cody Rhodes (who plays American GI Guile, flattop and all), and Hirooki Goto (sumo master E. Honda) to trained martial artists like Koji, Vidyut Jammwal (Dhalsim), and Alexander Volkanovski (Joe), which gives them a solidity that balances out all the impossible direct-from-the-game moves Sakurai folds in. When Ryu and Honda have a showdown in a steam-filled sauna, Honda leads off with his signature flying headbutt but also pummels his out-of-practice opponent with some bruising but plausible open-handed blows. With the exception of the sequences involving the CGI Blanka, the Brazilian beast-man performed by Jason Momoa, the movie avoids turning its bouts into physics-free encounters that look like they’re taking place inside a computer. It approaches them instead with the sensibility of a Hong Kong action movie in which characters might make wire-assisted leaps but also do plenty of battling within standard human capabilities. Chun-Li’s lighting kick is turned into something more realistic, while Russian grappler Zangief’s (Olivier Richters) piledriver is gleefully cartoonish. When the movie needs to go really outlandish, it turns to animated sequences à la Kill Bill.

Street Fighter is, more than anything, a ridiculous achievement in casting, which is also why it’s packed with characters we don’t get enough time with. It is flat-out inspired to cast country singer Orville Peck as masked Spanish fighter Vega, even if he’s barely around to sexually confound and then defeat Guile. 50 Cent, with a game-accurate and wild-looking hairline, makes for a worthy Balrog. (The only misstep is Andrew Schulz, whose sniveling Dan Hibiki gets way too much screen time for a character that adds nothing.) And Centineo is at his himbo best as the insecure Ken, psyching himself up by admiring his abs in the mirror, slipping around during a sock-footed skirmish with Ryu in a feat of fight choreography as slapstick, and toggling between self-aggrandizement and self-loathing. Street Fighter knows it is trash, wants to be trash, and aims for a ’90s direct-to-VHS-core vibe right down to its “to be continued” ending — which is only a shame because it occasionally achieves a kind of dumpster greatness despite itself, and there’s no reason why it couldn’t have tried for that the whole time.

When the Pentagon announced plans to livestream the execution of mass murderer Nidal Malik Hasan in December, the only surprise was that it hadn’t happened sooner. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth likes a little ultraviolence — inked on his body, in the form of Crusader tattoos, or the Scripture he quotes. “Blessed be the Lord, my rock, who trains my hands for war and my fingers for battle,” he intoned in a press briefing this spring, citing the Psalmist in defense of the war on Iran. In his imagination, he is the great champion of a “warrior culture,” by which he means masculinity or a homicidal version of it. He’s long defended war criminals like Clint Lorance, who ordered the murders of two Afghan civilians, and Eddie Gallagher, who reportedly stabbed a wounded, teenage ISIS fighter to death. So he chose to kill Hasan by firing squad — the first military execution in 65 years — and he wanted to show off for the world. A broadcast would remind the public that “there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” he told podcaster Jack Posobiec, an admirer of dictators Augusto Pinochet and Francisco Franco.

But Donald Trump apparently had misgivings, and on Thursday morning he said there would be no livestream. Hasan will still die by firing squad, he promised, and families of the victims can watch the killing in person, making this a conventional American execution after all. The impulses motivating Hegseth will not disappear so readily: Others share his lust for state brutality and, with it, the illusion of order. Although Hegseth’s planned livestream faced bipartisan criticism, the American right’s thirst for violent retribution has grown. Immigration authorities under Trump beat and shoot unarmed migrants, and in some cases they kill them. Trump has praised the Philippine ex-president Rodrigo Duterte, and his extrajudicial killings of thousands of alleged drug dealers, and wants to apply the death penalty more freely to anyone convicted of similar crimes. The modern right exploits a weakness in the American definition of justice, which looks more like vengeance.

By conventional American logic, Hasan deserves to die. The former Army psychiatrist and Islamic extremist killed 13 people on the Fort Hood military base in 2009, and injured 32 others, ahead of a deployment to Afghanistan. There have, of course, been “serious consequences” already: Law enforcement shot and paralyzed Hasan the day of his rampage, and he has spent the past 13 years on death row at Fort Leavenworth, awaiting the execution he said he desired. Hegseth was ready to grant his wish. Had Trump not intervened, U.S. soldiers would have shot Hasan to death while he was strapped into a wheelchair, for an audience of billions. The optics worried Trump more than the killing itself; only his “deep understanding of imagery” made him skeptical of a livestream, a source told CNN. There was no moral sensibility at work, only the vague sense that the public and bloody execution of a paralyzed man would reflect poorly on the administration.

Trump is right, in a way. The botched execution of Christa Pike took place behind curtains. Most state-sanctioned killings do. When the state does kill in the open, it rarely choreographs the carnage in the same, deliberate manner as the execution of Hasan. To date, “The various forms of televised death the administration has put out to this point have been abstract,” observed Marine veteran and novelist Phil Klay in the New York Times. The public might watch “a video feed of a building or boat and then an explosion,” he continued, but that’s not enough gore for Hegesth. To him, bloodshed is justice. Only by ordering soldiers to perforate a human being with bullets in front of us could he satisfy himself. Perhaps he thought that he is like everyone else; that we all long to watch a man bleed out in real time. Or that it would be good for us to do so, whether we realize it or not. Violence can become its own justification.

A few prominent conservatives agreed with Hegseth’s logic. Doug Wilson, who co-founded the Christian denomination to which Hegseth belongs, took issue with a livestream but not with public execution. If the government wants to hang Hasan in a stadium, that’s fine, he wrote on his blog, but it should not sell “popcorn and hot dogs” to the audience. “You obviously must have tickets, but they would have to be apportioned by lottery,” he mused. Palmer Luckey, a major Republican donor and the co-founder of Anduril Industries, said he has wanted “public executions for over a decade,” because they are the “ultimate example of the state’s monopoly on violence.” We should all “revel in the death of those who truly deserve it,” he added, for it is “aligned with our natural and national order.” Palantir co-founder and University of Austin founding chairman Joe Lonsdale concurred, saying, “Our society today is too soft in ways that cause our fellow citizens harm.”

Though most Americans opposed the livestream, just over half support the execution itself. If the U.S. has a national order, as Luckey suggested, it’s reflected by that number. We are one of the only developed nations in the world that still administers the death penalty. Although we’ve moved executions into the sterile environment of the prison death chamber, this was not always the case. Hasan’s public execution would have been the nation’s first since “the 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea,” CNN reported, “a Black man from Kentucky who was found guilty of raping a White woman by an all-White jury.” The Death Penalty Information Center says that 20,000 people gathered to watch Bethea die. Although history does not tell us if anyone sold popcorn and hot dogs, attendees could and did buy Coca-Cola and sandwiches. One spectator told reporters in 2016 that she was 5 years old when she watched Bethea die, and the sight haunted her for life. “I started having nightmares after I was older,” she said. “It’s like his spirit was just hanging all around me.”

There is a difference between a national order and a natural one. Most of us will never watch the condemned shake or hear their last breaths. “Do we really want to see?” asked Klay in the Times. For now, we don’t. Hegseth’s plan, the state killing as spectacle, tested our moral disposition — and found where it holds fast, and where it fails. The gap between what we accept and the truth we are prepared to confront benefits the most brutal among us. They can say that our justice is deficient. That we are incoherent, even cowardly, if we tolerate bloodshed but don’t want to perceive it. Had Hegseth won, and forced us to look, maybe we’d have nightmares, too. Maybe we should.
Typing with numb fingers, struggling to hold a pen, or waking with an aching hand can make everyday life exhausting for people with carpal tunnel syndrome.
The condition develops when a nerve supplying the hand becomes squeezed inside a narrow passage at the wrist. Pressure can disrupt the nerve's signals, causing pain, tingling, numbness, and weakness.
Now, a small trial has found that injecting saline around the trapped nerve could ease symptoms for longer than a steroid injection.
Relief persisted for six months after the saline procedure, by which time the initial benefits of steroid injection alone had largely faded.

The saline is used to open up space between tissues. In the procedure, called hydrodissection, a clinician uses ultrasound to guide a fine needle alongside the nerve. The sterile salt solution is injected around it, separating it from tissues that restrict its movement.
This aims to help the nerve move more freely. A steroid injection eases symptoms by reducing inflammation and swelling.

"This relieves the pressure on the nerve and improves patients' symptoms," radiologist Anupama Tandon, from University College of Medical Sciences and Guru Teg Bahadur Hospital in India, told ScienceAlert.

The researchers wanted to establish how much benefit came from separating the tissues. Most earlier hydrodissection studies included medication in the injected fluid, so it was hard to tell whether the procedure or the drug deserved the credit.

Led by radiologist Anindita Bose from Mahatma Gandhi Medical College and Hospital, the team studied 39 adults whose symptoms had persisted for more than three months, despite treatments such as medication or wrist splints.
Some had the condition in both hands, so the trial included 63 wrists.

Each wrist was randomly assigned to one of three treatments. One group received hydrodissection with saline alone. Another received a steroid injection without the tissue-separating procedure. The third received hydrodissection with steroid added to the saline.

All treatments were guided by ultrasound. The steroid-containing injections also included a local anesthetic. The researchers then followed changes in pain, numbness, and difficulty using the hand, with ultrasound scans checking nerve swelling during the first three months.
All three treatments helped initially. The difference emerged over the following months: Pain returned in the steroid-only group, while relief continued in the saline-only hydrodissection group.
Adding steroid to hydrodissection did not clearly improve the results.
Ultrasound images supported the patients' reports. Nerve swelling decreased more in both hydrodissection groups than in the group given steroid injections alone.

These findings support the researchers' explanation that separating the nerve from surrounding tissues contributes to relief. However, the trial had no group that received a dummy injection, so the contribution of patients' treatment expectations could not be assessed separately.
Tandon described a young typist whose pain and numbness had become so disruptive that her job was at risk. Medication and a wrist splint had failed to help.
"Post hydrodissection, she had improvement in her symptoms and was able to resume her work," Tandon said.

Treatment took around 15 minutes and required no hospital stay. No major complications were observed. Some participants experienced mild pain and swelling that settled within a few days. One experienced tingling during needle placement, with no lasting neurological effects reported.

Larger studies are needed to establish how reliably the procedure works and how long relief lasts. This trial involved a small number of people at one center, with follow-up ending at six months. It did not directly compare hydrodissection with surgery.
"It is beneficial for mild to moderate CTS [carpal tunnel syndrome]," Tandon said, "while severe cases require surgery."
The team has begun a longer study comparing saline with dextrose, a type of sugar, to investigate which fluid provides more lasting relief.
The research has been published in Radiology.

Almost a decade ago, the Air Force created Kessel Run in 2017 as a military-commercial partnership and Airmen-led “software factory” in response to the service’s troubled rollout of the Air Operations Center 10.2.

The name, a nod to the Star Wars movie franchise, references a smuggling route that hero Han Solo bragged about making in “12 parsecs.” It also served as a reminder for Airmen coders to move fast and overcome complex software demands under intense pressure and tight timelines through bureaucratic obstacles, much like the space monsters, asteroids, gravity distortions, and stellar anomalies that often doomed pilots attempting to make the Kessel Run.

The program scored early wins with “Jigsaw,” a cloud-based tanker aircraft planning application, and spawned a network of software factories across the Air Force. NATO adopted Jigsaw in 2020, and planners used the first cloud-generated Air Tasking Order via the Kessel Run All Domain Operations Suite, KRADOS. Personnel also injected real-time software updates for command-and-control work during the chaotic U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in August 2021.
A month later, Kessel Run signed a formal user agreement with Air Combat Command that put the fledgling but successful organization into the Pentagon’s software acquisition pathway.

Then, in 2025, Kessel Run shifted from its small teams of Active-duty Coders to a “government-led, vendor-managed” model. This February, KR kicked off its most ambitious efforts yet under the new model, an effort to create the “next generation” of the Air Operations Centers that integrate artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data fusion.

Col. Brian Viola took the helm at Kessel Run in June and is now charged with taking the baton from past leaders while sprinting ahead as the Air Force seeks a modernized AOC to serve as the key nodes in its updated command and control network.

Viola has spent his career at the Air Force Research Laboratory, National Security Agency, and the Idaho National Laboratory, and previously served as commander of the 346th Test Squadron at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas, which runs independent operational testing and evaluation of cyber capabilities. He also served as the inaugural leader of the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s “Platform One,” also based in San Antonio, the Department of the Air Force entity that provides Development, Security, and Operations as a service.
Viola sat down recently with Air & Space Forces Magazine to talk about where Kessel Run has been and where it’s headed.
Editor’s Note: This Q&A has been edited for length and clarity
Q: What has changed for the mission of Kessel Run since its shift from an Airmen-led software factory to its life for nearly the past two years as a “government-led, vendor-managed” model?

A: I would not say that Kessel Run’s mission has changed at all. But as far as organic delivery for Kessel Run, we’re no longer a software factory. Our mission is to deliver the AOC weapons system. What does that look like in a software-defined future? How do we iteratively deliver capability in that space? Kessel Run has had several transitions. Most notably is the pivot from organic, software delivery, blue-suited developers doing code to a contractor-led model today.
Q: What changed that led to this transition?

A: If you rewind five to eight years, the acquisition transformation has also drastically changed the landscape. Technology has changed as well. In a previous job at Platform One, we were standing up the first really [Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery] pipeline within the Department of Defense to deliver software at speed. Industry has kind of latched onto that. That’s a commodity these days. There are vendors downstairs; you could just go buy a platform today. You could kind of even see that in cloud space over the past, you know, eight to 10 years, where you had [Defense Information System Agency], private clouds. Now you can just go purchase that as a commodity. I think from a Kessel Run standpoint, what we’ve really done is we’ve just changed to adapt to the current landscape.
Q: With modernizing the AOC, are there other partners, allies, industry or commercial operations that USAF can draw on for ideas?

A: I’m in the planning stages of going to check out an airline’s global operations center. I don’t know whether the answer is that industry already does what AOCs do, or whether airlines do that, but they manage tens of thousands of flights a day. They deal with weather around the globe. They deal with pilots and flight attendants who get sick. They have a snowstorm and have to optimize for tomorrow by repositioning their aircraft in the right places. They’re optimizing for fuel costs and passengers. The real question that I have is: are the tools to do that and [the tools] the AOC needs drastically different? Can we use the same algorithms with different weights to optimize for different things?
Q: How does AI fit into what Kessel Run is trying to do with the AOCs?

A: I think there are two places where AI is very applicable. One is accelerating capability production, capability delivery, and partnering with the defense industrial base. We can leverage that smartly. And the other place is: how do you integrate that into operations? We’re in constant conversation with the AOC commanders, with [Air Combat Command], and even at the Department of the Air Force level on what’s available. What is enterprise-level? What can we leverage, and then how do we apply it to the problem set? If somebody has a new capability, I’m not going to turn a blind eye. If the Department of War has a capability we can leverage against a problem set, then I think Kessel Run has the right culture to push boundaries where needed to deliver that capability to the warfighter.

Q: The Air Force recently announced that Kessel Run had partnered with Air Combat Command and Air Education and Training Command on the Aerospace Readiness Enterprise System aimed at aircrew readiness. What should we know about ARES and how it relates to AOC modernization?

A: Where I find it very interesting is when you look at that problem set of aircrew readiness through a larger lens that includes the AOC, fully acknowledging that aircrew readiness during peacetime looks one way, and another during war, but many of the fundamentals remain during times of war. For instance, you need to have crew rest. You need to be able to turn maintenance on platforms. People need to be certified. You need to get people in and out of theater. When we talk about dynamic mission replanning in the AOC, that’s often weighted by what assets you have available. Optimizing those assets will be paramount. But if you optimize your assets agnostic of what you’re trying to accomplish, and vice versa, you’re probably going to come up with some kind of suboptimal solution. What we’re trying to do is drive synergies across that space. While we’re trying to do aircrew readiness, and that in itself is a problem to solve, we are also keeping an eye on how we operate in a dynamic environment, not just on day-to-day operations, which is dynamic enough, but also in wartime operations, and trying to pull those two together.
SpaceX will fly its uncrewed reentry Starfall capsule aboard the Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, scheduled for launch before dawn on Monday.

The 32 payloads onboard the Falcon 9 rocket will take flight from Space Launch Complex 40 during an hour-long window that opens at 6:30 a.m. EDT (1030 UTC). The rocket will fly on a southeasterly trajectory upon leaving the pad.

The 45th Weather Squadron forecast a 55 percent chance for acceptable weather during the launch window, stating that a cold front along southern Florida will bring gusty winds at liftoff that are “approaching constraints” to launch. There is also a moderate to high risk that weather at the recovery site for the first stage booster won’t be acceptable.

“Occasional coastal showers are also possible within the persistent onshore flow, although these are expected to be shallow and low-topped, with some more stratiform in nature,” launch weather officers wrote in a prelaunch forecast. “Therefore, the Cumulus Cloud Rule is a secondary concern.”

SpaceX will launch the mission using the Falcon 9 first stage booster with the tail number B1085. This will be its 19th flight following the launches of NASA’s Crew-9, Fram2, Firefly Blue Ghost Mission 1, RRT-1, SXM-10, SXM-11, MTG-S1, EchoStar25, and 10 batches of Starlink satellites.

Nearly nine minutes after liftoff, B1085 will target a landing on the droneship, A Shortall of Gravitas. If successful, this will be the 167th landing on this vessel and the 672nd Falcon booster landing to date.

Beyond SpaceX’s Starfall capsule, 20 of the remaining 31 payloads to be deployed were manifested by multinational mission management company, Exolaunch. Those include four radio-frequency monitoring satellites from Virginia-based, HawkEye 360; four communications satellites for Finnish micro satellite company, Iceye; and six navigation satellites from California-based, Xona Space Systems.

SpaceX first debuted its reentry capsule called Starfall back in June. During that mission, SpaceX played its cards close to the vest, not revealing that its spacecraft was onboard the rocket until fairly close to flight.
Even at that, the company just shared a rendering of the vehicle and didn’t disclose during its launch broadcast when it would be deployed.

“SpaceX has developed a new spacecraft called Starfall, which at its core is a microgravity lab researchers and entrepreneurs can leverage to develop their products and innovations, said Zachary Luppen, an avionics supply chain engineer at SpaceX and the commentator during the June 23 broadcast.
“As we have seen demonstrated on the International Space Station, there is a huge opportunity to benefit life here on Earth through microgravity research and in-space manufacturing”

The Federal Aviation Administration noted in an environmental assessment of Starfall that the vehicle is about 0.75 meters (2.5 feet) tall, 3.1 meters (10.2 feet) in diameter, and has a mass of about 2,100 kilograms (4,600 pounds). The FAA said a single Starfall capsule has the ability to support up to 1,000 kilograms (2,200 pounds) of payload mass.
SpaceX didn’t state what, if any, payloads were onboard this Starfall mission.

SpaceX’s Starfall isn’t the only reentry vehicle onboard the Bandwagon-5 mission. Varda Space Industries, which focuses on pharmaceutical research missions, is launching its W-Series 7 spacecraft, which is about three times smaller than Starfall.

Despite the name, W-7 will be Varda’s ninth reentry capsule launched to date. W-8 and W-9 were launched earlier this month on the Transporter-18 mission. W-7 features the cancer drug called Protac and will study whether microgravity can improve its solubility.

“In microgravity, molecules can crystallize differently than they do on Earth, potentially producing crystal forms with improved properties, including better solubility,” Varda wrote on its website prior to launch. “If successful, the experiment could help turn powerful protein-degrading molecules into more practical and effective cancer treatments.”
Also onboard Bandwagon-5 is the Starburst-1 demo mission from Portal Space Systems Inc. The 260 kg spacecraft is designed to perform orbital maneuvers and support a customer payload of up to 50 kg.

This first demonstration of the Starburst spacecraft is “fully funded by Portal to prove capability ahead of customer missions,” the company said on its website. Customer flights are advertised as starting in 2027.

A NASA-funded air pollution monitoring network has provided one of the most detailed long-term views yet of the role of black carbon, or soot produced by fires, diesel vehicles, and other combustion sources, in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa. The detailed measurements show how pollution changes by time of day and season, including increases associated with rush-hour traffic and holiday celebrations. The findings are relevant to cities around the world, including in the United States.

In a new paper published in ES&T: Air, scientists analyzed data collected throughout Addis Ababa between 2022 and 2025 from 10 air-quality monitoring sites deployed by NASA’s Multi-Angle Imager for Aerosols (MAIA) project.

The research comes as Ethiopia is taking steps aimed at improving air quality. In 2024, the country became the first in the world to ban the import of internal combustion engine vehicles, while cities have been adding bike lanes and electric vehicle infrastructure. The MAIA project’s measurements provide researchers with a baseline for understanding how air quality changes over time as Addis Ababa continues to grow and evolve.

The study focuses on particulate matter that is 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter, also known as PM2.5. The 2025 State of Global Air Report, cited in the paper, estimates that exposure to PM2.5 is associated with approximately 4.9 million deaths globally each year. Among the many kinds of PM2.5, black carbon has been has been studied for its potential effects on human health.

The paper found that Addis Ababa’s three-year average PM2.5 concentration was 30 micrograms per cubic meter, which is more than three times the level of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s health-based annual PM2.5 standard. The new paper cites data from MAIA’s ground sensors indicating that average black carbon levels in Addis Ababa were approximately four to nine times higher than those measured in the three U.S. metropolitan areas the mission is monitoring.

“To our knowledge, this is the first long-term, multisite study of continuous PM2.5 and black carbon measurements in Ethiopia,” said Sina Hasheminassab, a coauthor of the paper and MAIA’s deputy principal investigator at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “Many rapidly growing cities have limited long-term monitoring, so these measurements provide an important baseline for understanding how pollution changes across space and time.”

The composition and sources of PM2.5 can differ substantially between cities, depending on their local geography, traffic, industries, and more. Desert cities, for example, may have more dust, while those near coal-fired power plants may have higher concentrations of sulfate. Long-term surface measurements remain limited in many parts of the world.

NASA is supporting MAIA’s air pollution research in a dozen metropolitan areas around the globe, including three in the U.S.: Los Angeles, Atlanta, and Boston. The mission consists of a ground-based network of sensors already in operation as well as a space observatory, which uses a JPL-built camera that will be launched by the Italian Space Agency (ASI) on an ASI satellite no earlier than late 2027.

The camera is designed to identify different types of PM2.5 aerosols based on how they reflect light, making it possible to map particle concentrations over each city that the mission studies. Mounted on a gimbal, the camera captures data from multiple angles using JPL-pioneered technologies that make particles stand out more prominently against the surface background to provide valuable information about their shape and size.

The MAIA mission is the first NASA project to include public health researchers among a space mission’s team. These researchers will use MAIA’s PM2.5 concentration maps alongside health data to study potential relationships between different particle types and health outcomes. By developing a better understanding of particulate matter pollution, researchers can potentially advance how air quality is studied and managed.

“This paper shows how valuable the air sensor data is on its own, but combining the sensor network and satellite observations will be a game-changer,” said, Kyan Shlipak, the paper’s lead author, who worked on the research while interning at JPL.
The greater Addis Ababa urban area is home to nearly 6 million people, and according to United Nations projections, that figure is expected to surpass 10 million by 2050.

“It’s a cosmopolitan city with many international communities,” said Araya Asfaw of Addis Ababa University, a coauthor of the paper and the MAIA project’s lead Ethiopian collaborator. “Think of it as Africa’s version of Brussels, where the European Union is based.”
“Even at night, when traffic dies down, you see high emissions from the burning of charcoal and other fuels,” Asfaw said.

The MAIA sensor network detected increases in black carbon during two major holidays in Addis Ababa that involve bonfires and was able to distinguish between particles originating from the fires and those from fossil fuel combustion. The findings demonstrate how detailed measurements can help researchers identify different sources of particulate matter and better understand how air quality varies across a city and over time.
