Songwriting has long been at the core of music, and for a time, it was one of the surest ways to make a living. Today’s industry, driven by streams and fractional royalty rates, has made it harder for writers to sustain the craft, but that won’t stop the talented from trying.

The boom in podcasts about song creation proves songcraft has universal appeal. Some episodes put recognizable names and faces in the guest seat, but many spotlight the unseen creatives behind the scenes.

Although you don’t have to be a musician to ask how it’s done, many of these podcasts are hosted by professional songwriters. What they share is an emphasis on the relentless hard work it takes to land a first hit, and the continued graft to keep the momentum going. The message is clear: it’s not glamorous, but once a song connects with people, it’s totally worth it.
Here are seven songwriting podcasts we recommend, ordered by launch date from longest-running to newest.

Liverpool-based musician duo Simon Barber and Brian O’Connor, professionally known as Sodajerker, have been hosting the Sodajerker on Songwriting podcast for 15 years. Delving deep into the songwriting process with classic and current creators, they have welcomed Paul McCartney, Paul Simon, Jimmy Webb, and Todd Rundgren and, more recently, Chaka Khan and Phil Collins. Episodes focus on specific landmark songs while also spotlighting each guest’s current release, and often providing revealing insight. The award-winning podcast spawned the BBC World Service documentary The Secrets of Songwriting, and as of 2020, its interview archive is housed at the British Library.

Hrishikesh Hirway’s Song Exploder is many music lovers’ gateway podcast to the songwriting world. Launched in 2014, the series has more than 300 episodes, each dissecting a single song in under half an hour. An accomplished musician who has released albums as The One AM Radio, Hirway turned to podcasting after a bout of writer’s block, hoping to find a breakthrough in fellow musicians’ creative processes. The popular show took on a life of its own, however, becoming his day job and spawning a Netflix series. It goes from strength to strength with recent guests like Elvis Costello, Olivia Rodrigo, and Charli XCX.

Podcasters turned authors Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding have been examining Top 40 songs since 2014 to decipher why they became hits and what we, as listeners, are responding to. A professor of musicology and a songwriter/music educator, respectively, the pair’s approach is both academic and forensic. Episodes sometimes feature artists, among them Carly Rae Jepsen, Tove Lo, and Lizzy McAlpine. More often, the two analyze the music in granular detail. The series spawned a book, Switched On Pop: How Popular Music Works and Why It Matters (2019), and the podcast is featured on Netflix.

Being featured on And the Writer Is… has become a badge of honor for song creators. Hosted by acclaimed songwriter Ross Golan, who has penned hits for Selena Gomez, Jason Derulo, and Celine Dion, the weekly podcast offers a peek behind the scenes at how the song sausage is made. Guests have included Finneas, Bebe Rexha, Ryan Tedder, and Ziggy Marley. Geared toward music professionals and fans alike, the series has more than 250 episodes. Running over an hour, each conversation unpacks the songwriting process and the guest’s musical journey, focusing as much on the hard times as the successes.

Songwriters on Process zeroes in on the writing more than the song, understandable given its host, Ben Opipari, holds a PhD in English language and literature. The project began in 2010 as written interviews with songwriters and evolved in 2022 into a podcast about writers talking about writing, which could apply to songs or books. His far-reaching guest list runs from Julia Jacklin, Rostam, and Jason Newsted to Lucius and Death Cab for Cutie’s Ben Gibbard. What sets the podcast apart is that Opipari is not a songwriter, but his love for music and the writing process is apparent in his thorough interview style.

Geared toward established and burgeoning songwriters, Songwriter Soup, hosted by Grammy-nominated songwriter Laura Veltz, is an invaluable resource. The industry- and lifestyle-focused podcast serves as an audio handbook for songwriters, sharing best practices and insider pro tips for surviving and thriving in this difficult-to-navigate creative space. Among the experts Veltz has welcomed are Tayla Parx, Gabe Simon, and Joybeth Taylor who kicked off the series’ fifth season. This season also marks Songwriter Soup as an official nonprofit, expanding its reach beyond conversation to practical ways for songwriters to protect themselves professionally and personally.

Justin Tranter could have retired long ago, having penned multiple billion-streaming hits such as Justin Bieber’s “Sorry,” Imagine Dragons’ “Believer,” and Chappell Roan’s “Good Luck, Babe!” Instead, the Grammy nominee has expanded his reach into various fields, including the podcast Unfamous, where he chats with shapers of pop culture, including industry decision-makers and music creators. Guests come in pairs: the celebrity, so to speak, and the collaborator who helped get them where they are. Launched earlier this year, the podcast has already dissected the careers of Katy Perry, Melanie Martinez, Troye Sivan, and Debbie Gibson, among others.
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for the Oct. 18 episode of “The Simpsons,” “The Revengening,” which aired Sunday night on Fox.

“The Simpsons” has pulled off its own October surprise: Apu Nahasapeemapetilon is back. The fan favorite character finally spoke again for the first time in nearly a decade on Sunday night’s episode, “The Revengening.” Variety has exclusively learned who is behind Apu’s new voice: actor and voice-over vet Sunil Malhotra (“Grey’s Anatomy,” “The Legend of Korra”).

Malhotra’s hiring and the return of Apu — who has been seen, but not heard on “The Simpsons” since the October 2017 episode “The Serfsons” — was a closely guarded secret inside “The Simpsons” universe. Fox didn’t share a screener for “The Revengening,” and producers kept both the episode’s table read and its subsequent production under tight protocols (including NDAs for all involved).

Also heard on Sunday’s episode was the debut of Janina Gavankar (“The Morning Show”) as Apu’s wife, Manjula. And now that Apu is back and the Kwik-E-Mart has reopened, executive producer Matt Selman said both characters and the Nahasapeemapetilon family will once again be seen (and heard) on “The Simpsons” more often.

“We love this character, and wanted to bring him back in a smart, ‘Simpsons’-y way that allowed him to evolve,” Selman said. “We’re excited by what Sunil has already brought to the role, and look forward to seeing more of Apu in the future.”

Hank Azaria previously voiced Apu, a character that has been controversial over the years due to its stereotypical portrayal of a South Asian convenience store clerk. The issue of Apu was the centerpiece of the 2017 documentary “The Problem With Apu,” in which comedian Hari Kondabolu discussed the impact the character has had on people of South Asian descent.

After that doc made waves — including in “The Simpsons” writers’ room, where it was screened and discussed — Azaria announced that he would no longer voice Apu. “I apologize for my part in creating that and participating in that,” Azaria said in 2021 on Dax Shepard’s podcast “Armchair Expert.” “Part of me feels like I need to go to every single Indian person in this country and personally apologize. And sometimes I do.”

In the aftermath, Apu was shifted to the background on “The Simpsons,” as producers decided how to handle the character going forward. For years, that meant Apu would still occasionally be seen in Springfield, but never heard.

Until now. The idea of bringing back Apu this way, as one of this year’s Halloween-themed episodes, came from staffer Nick Dahan (who’s the credited writer on “The Revengening”) and co-executive producer Cesar Mazariegos. After hearing their pitch, Selman said he thought it was “a brilliant way” to bring Apu back and reference the entire situation.
Voice actor Malhotra said he took time to look into what it would mean to take over Apu and talked to the producers to make sure the character was more culturally appropriate.

“When my agent called me about a ‘Simpsons’ audition, I knew exactly what role it was for, and the idea actually made my stomach sink,” he said. “But admittedly, part of me was also curious. It had been eight years since Apu had spoken on the show, and it got me thinking: Did the writers’ room look different now? Could they bring him back in a way that acknowledged and apologized for past mistakes? Could I make the character my own, and reclaim him in some way? And could they achieve all of that in an unmistakably ‘Simpsons’ way that didn’t disappoint fans?

“Whether the producers knew it or not, I was prepared to walk away,” he continued. Malhotra said that he declined his very first “professional job offer 28 years ago” because it would have required him to play a stereotypical “Hindu guy,” adding that playing such a caricature “to be the butt of the joke wasn’t something I was willing to do, and I’ve turned down similar work multiple times since.”

But as Malhotra got further down the road with “The Simpsons,” he said, he began engaging with the producers about their plans for Apu before he would commit to the role, where he was promised that the return of Apu was being handled with the utmost care.

“My callback was the first of many times that no one at ‘The Simpsons’ let me down,” he said. “I told casting that I’d only consider an offer if I could meet showrunner Matt Selman and co-executive producer Cesar Mazariegos, both of whom gladly did so. It was the beginning of a deeply collaborative experience that I hope is equally satisfying for longtime fans of ‘The Simpsons’ and for other South Asian kids who, like me, stopped watching at some point along the way.”

In “The Revengening,” a spooky lead-up to next week’s “Treehouse of Horror XXXVII,” a man in a “Daft Monk” Halloween costume (as in, a Daft Punk helmet and monastic robe — wordplay!) is accidentally killed over and over again by Springfield residents all over town. A year later, “Daft Monk” is still alive, and getting his revenge by taking out his would-be killers, one by one.
Eventually “Daft Monk” summons the townspeople to Springfield City Hall, where he takes his helmet off and reveals that he’s actually Apu.

“I’d be lying if I didn’t say that the sweetest part of all was unleashing that righteously rage-fueled “I AM APU!” — on behalf of so many of us — over and over in the studio until we got it just right,” Malhotra said. “I really feel like we did and I can’t wait for fans to see more Apu.”

Apu then shares his backstory: After he was nearly killed dozens of times, he wound up on “The Island of Forgotten Garbage,” where he’s healed by “The Simpsons” quack Dr. Nick (who also has been seen sparingly in recent years). “All the junk Springfield gets rid of winds up here,” he tells Apu, “like you … If you wound up here, it’s for a reason, right, Leon?” (Out pops the character that Michael Jackson played in the Season 3 episode “Stark Raving Mad,” which was pulled from “Simpsons” rotation in 2019 after the doc “Leaving Neverland” showcased more allegations against the late pop star.)
Says Apu before he reveals himself: “I am the man you left for dead. I am the one you pretended never existed!”

Then, unmasked, he tells the Springfield crowd: “It would have been so easy to bring me back. I immediately ran home to my family, but they were gone. Then I went to the Kwik-E-Mart, and was shocked to find it abandoned. As I wandered aimlessly through town, no one even noticed me. It was as if I was invisible. That was when I vowed to take my revenge on Springfield.”

He’s about to light City Hall on fire, but Marge Simpson pipes up — representing the Springfield citizens, but also clearly serving as a mouthpiece for the show’s producers: “Apu, we’re so sorry we left you for dead. Believe me, we wanted to do the right thing.”
Bart adds: “But we were so scared, and just didn’t know what to do.”
Lenny also chimes in, in a nod to the debates inside “The Simpsons” writers’ room: “If it’s any consolation, we had so many internal conversations about it.”
But, Carl finishes, “Ahh, they kind of just didn’t go anywhere.” (And for almost a decade, that’s how “The Simpsons” never got around to bringing back Apu.)

Homer then offers to sacrifice himself to save the rest of the town, and offers this penance to Apu, while reminding viewers how important Apu has been to the makeup of Springfield: “I’m just doing what the old Apu would have done. The guy who loved this town and everyone in it. You were on our bowling teams, our barbershop quartets, our dad rock cover bands. We took you for granted. I took you for granted.”

But before Apu can blow up the town, he wakes up. It turns out it was a nightmare; no one is dead. He’s back in the Kwik E-Mart, and Manjula is there too. So is his No. 1 customer, Homer, who invites him to a Halloween party.
“What the heck? I’ll do it,” Apu says. “A Halloween party sounds kind of fun. Plus, I feel like I haven’t seen everyone in ages. Oh, but I wish I had a costume.”
But he actually does: There’s a “Daft Monk” costume stashed under the cash register. So was it really a dream? And that’s the end of the episode — but Apu is back!

This isn’t the first time “The Simpsons” writers used their characters to allude to their indecisiveness on what to do with Apu. In the 2018 episode “No Good Read Goes Unpunished,” Marge begins reading her favorite childhood novel to Lisa, but quickly realizes the old book was a lot more offensive and racist than she remembered. She tries to sanitize it, but “now it’s as inoffensive as a Sunday in Cincinnati … what am I supposed to do?”

Lisa then looks at the audience, seemingly addressing “Simpsons” fans: “It’s hard to say. Something that started decades ago and was applauded and inoffensive is now politically incorrect. What can you do?”

The scene pulls back to reveal a photo of Apu near Lisa’s bed, and it’s obvious they’re no longer talking about a book, but their own show. With Marge also looking straight at viewers, the two suggest that “Some things will be dealt with at a later date … if at all.” (It should be noted that Apu and his children also appeared in the episode, but did not speak.)

In June 2020, during the post-George Floyd reckoning on race, “The Simpsons” announced that moving forward, its characters of color would be voiced by culturally appropriate actors. Among the major changes, Alex Désert took over as Carl Carlson from Azaria, and Kevin Michael Richardson (who had already been a part of the series cast) became Dr. Julius Hibbert, which was previously Harry Shearer. Now, Apu, with Malhotra taking over, joins that list as well.

And for several years, the creative team promised that they would address Apu at some point. In 2021, series creator Matt Groening told USA Today that the producers were first seeing if they could make new Apu stories work. “I think the Apu stories are fantastic, and he’s one of the most nuanced characters on a silly two-dimensional cartoon show,” Groening said in the interview.

Early reactions on social media about the return of Apu has already been positive: “Apu is back thank you Simpsons,” said one. Another: “The Simpsons reveals the new voice for Apu. Representation for Indian Americans. Well played Matt Groening and Dan Castellaneta, Hank Azaria, Nancy Cartwright, Harry Shearer, Julie Kavner and Yeardley Smith.” Wrote a third: “Apu reveal is the greatest thing to happen on the Simpsons in a long time. I missed that genius character!”

Malhotra’s recent voice credits include “The Legend of Vox Machina,” “The Loud House,” “Monster High,” “The Casagrandes” and “Star Wars: Tales of the Jedi.” He’s also been heard on video games including “Mortal Kombat 1,” “Avatar: The Last Airbender – Quest of Balance” and “Marvel’s Avengers.” In TV, besides “Grey’s Anatomy,” he’s also appeared on “ER,” “NCIS: New Orleans,” “MacGyver” and “Maron.”
Scientists link a strange sugar in red meat to a 63% higher diabetes risk

- A study of nearly 90,000 adults found that people consuming the most of a little-known sugar found in red meat had a 63% higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Scientists suspect the sugar may trigger chronic inflammation, potentially revealing a hidden connection between red meat and diabetes that goes beyond weight gain.

A sugar naturally present in red meat may help explain why eating these foods has been associated with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. Preliminary findings from a large observational study suggest that people who consume the most of this sugar face a substantially greater risk of developing the disease, potentially because of its effects on the immune system and chronic inflammation.

The sugar, known as N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc), is particularly common in beef and lamb. Researchers found that participants with the highest intake of meat-derived Neu5Gc had a 63% higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes (T2D) compared with those who consumed the least.

The association remained statistically significant after researchers accounted for several established diabetes risk factors, including physical activity, overall diet, smoking, and existing health conditions. It became weaker after body mass index (BMI) was also considered, but remained significant.
The findings were presented at the Annual Meeting of The European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy.

“Our findings support chronic inflammation as a specific mechanism linking red meat consumption with T2D, partly beyond the amount of red meat a person eats and partly independent of body fat,” said lead author Dr. Leopold Fezeu from the Université Sorbonne Paris Nord, Bobigny, France.
The researchers also observed that diabetes risk generally increased with greater consumption of meat-derived Neu5Gc, particularly among those with the highest exposure.
“Although we do not know exactly what levels of Neu5Gc trigger an immune response, our data suggest that higher intakes of meat-derived Neu5Gc are associated with a progressively higher risk of T2D.”
Why a Sugar in Red Meat May Trigger Inflammation

Neu5Gc is produced naturally by most mammals, but humans lost the ability to make it following an ancient mutation in the CMAH gene. Despite this evolutionary change, the sugar can still enter the human body through food.
It occurs in red meat (particularly beef and lamb), with smaller amounts also found in dairy products.

After Neu5Gc is consumed, the body absorbs it and can incorporate it into human tissues. Because humans do not naturally produce the molecule, the immune system may recognize it as foreign. Scientists classify it as a xeno-autoantigen, a foreign substance that becomes incorporated into the body's own tissues and can provoke an immune reaction.

In response, the immune system produces antibodies against Neu5Gc. The resulting prolonged immune activity, called xenosialitis (xenosialitis), has previously been associated with cardiovascular disease and cancer.

Researchers suspect that this persistent inflammatory response could also contribute to type 2 diabetes. However, before this investigation, no large prospective study had examined whether dietary Neu5Gc might promote diabetes through chronic inflammation.
Nearly 90,000 Adults Studied Over Several Years

To investigate the possible connection, the scientists analyzed dietary and health information from 89,953 adults participating in NutriNet-Santé, a large French observational study that follows people over time to examine how nutrition and lifestyle influence health.
Participants were 42 years old on average, and 79% were women. None had type 2 diabetes or cancer when they entered the study.

Each person completed three 24-hour dietary records. The research team then used a validated food database to calculate how much Neu5Gc participants were likely consuming based on the measured amounts of the sugar in different foods.

The analysis included a broad range of red meats, such as beef, lamb, pork, rabbit, goat, and game. Processed meats (such as bacon, sausages and cured meats) were evaluated as a separate category, while dairy products were analyzed independently.

Using the dietary information, the researchers estimated total Neu5Gc intake from all reported foods. They then ranked participants separately by sex according to their intake of meat-derived Neu5Gc and divided them into five equally sized groups (quintiles).
Diabetes risk was compared across these groups, using those with the lowest intake as the reference.
During a median follow-up period of 7.2 years, researchers recorded 966 new cases of type 2 diabetes.
Higher Red Meat Sugar Intake Linked to 63% Greater Diabetes Risk

The results showed a significant relationship between meat-derived Neu5Gc consumption and the likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes. The association became particularly pronounced among participants with the highest estimated intake.

Compared with the lowest intake group, individuals in the highest group had a 63% greater risk of developing the disease. Those in the second-highest group had a 41% greater risk (men and women combined).
These estimates accounted for potentially influential factors, including age, sex, exercise habits, overall dietary quality, smoking, and existing medical conditions.
The researchers also examined how much meat participants typically consumed.
Among men in the highest Neu5Gc intake group, median red meat consumption was 97 grams daily (136 g including processed meat). For women, the corresponding amount was 73 grams (96 g).
By comparison, men in the lowest intake group consumed a median of just 5 grams of red meat per day (21 g), while women consumed 0 grams (9 g).
The relationship between Neu5Gc and diabetes was observed in both sexes, with no statistically significant evidence that it differed between men and women (see tables in notes to editors).
The findings were also consistent when differences in total calorie intake were considered.

Researchers noticed that the increase in diabetes risk was especially steep at higher levels of Neu5Gc exposure. One possible explanation is that the immune system begins to respond more strongly after enough of the foreign sugar has accumulated in body tissues, although this proposed threshold mechanism has not been confirmed.

Importantly, when the analysis additionally accounted for the total amount of red meat consumed, the relationship between Neu5Gc and diabetes weakened and was no longer statistically significant. The direction of the association remained the same, however.

This means the researchers cannot determine whether Neu5Gc itself (rather than other components of red meat) is responsible for the increased risk. The findings suggest it could contribute to the relationship, but they do not establish that the sugar acts independently of red meat consumption.
Diabetes Risk May Extend Beyond Weight Gain
Another notable finding was that obesity appeared to explain only a relatively small portion of the association.
According to the researchers' estimates, obesity accounted for approximately 13% of the relationship between meat-derived Neu5Gc consumption and type 2 diabetes.
This suggests that factors unrelated to excess body weight may contribute substantially to the observed connection.

One possibility is that immune reactions to Neu5Gc produce chronic inflammation that interferes with insulin-producing cells or tissues that normally respond to insulin. Such effects could potentially increase the likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes even without substantial weight gain.
However, additional studies are necessary to establish whether these inflammatory processes actually explain the association.
Why Dairy Products Showed Different Results
Although Neu5Gc occurs in both red meat and dairy products, the researchers found an important difference between these dietary sources.
Higher consumption of Neu5Gc from dairy products was not associated with an increased risk of type 2 diabetes.

This finding may reflect the relatively small amounts of Neu5Gc in cow's milk compared with red meats such as beef and lamb. The typically smaller amounts of Neu5Gc consumed through dairy servings may also contribute to the difference.

When the scientists considered Neu5Gc intake from all dietary sources combined, participants in the highest intake group had a 37% greater risk of developing type 2 diabetes compared with those in the lowest group.
That association appeared to be driven primarily by Neu5Gc obtained from red meat.

“Together, these findings suggest that the association between Neu5Gc and T2D may depend on its dietary source, with meat-derived Neu5Gc showing a stronger association with T2D risk than total dietary Neu5Gc,” said Dr. Fezeu. “There may be differences between sources, or other components of red meat may contribute.”
Could Changing Protein Sources Lower Diabetes Risk?
The findings raise the possibility that reducing dietary exposure to meat-derived Neu5Gc could eventually become one approach to lowering diabetes risk.
However, researchers emphasize that studies are still needed to determine whether replacing foods rich in Neu5Gc with other protein sources would actually produce measurable health benefits.

“Given how common red meat is in Western diets, the strong association between meat-derived Neu5Gc and T2D risk is an important finding. Future research should explore whether reducing exposure to meat-derived Neu5Gc, for example by favoring poultry or plant-based proteins over beef and lamb, which have the highest Neu5Gc content, could help prevent T2D. Studies directly measuring anti-Neu5Gc antibodies in large cohorts would also help to directly test the xenosialitis mechanism in humans.”

The research team plans to investigate how Neu5Gc interacts with other substances found in red meat, including heme iron (a form of dietary iron), and how these components may collectively relate to diabetes risk.

They also intend to measure antibodies against Neu5Gc directly. Doing so could help determine whether the proposed immune response is an important biological mechanism connecting red meat consumption with type 2 diabetes.
The researchers caution that their findings are preliminary and have not yet been validated. The reported estimates could change once the final analysis is completed.
Because the study was observational, it cannot establish that Neu5Gc causes type 2 diabetes or identify precisely which factors are responsible for the higher risk.
Although the analysis accounted for several established diabetes risk factors, unmeasured lifestyle and social influences could still have affected the results.

There were also limitations in how dietary exposure was assessed. Neu5Gc consumption was estimated using participants' food records rather than measured directly, and the researchers did not account for possible dietary changes during the follow-up period. Both factors could have introduced errors into the exposure estimates.

The findings therefore offer a potential new explanation for the established connection between red meat consumption and diabetes, but further investigation is needed to determine whether Neu5Gc directly contributes to the disease.

Dad shift: Men now file majority of paid family leave claims in key states
The U.S. has no law guaranteeing paid parental leave. But in states with their own programs, more dads are using the benefit to bond with their new children, exceeding moms in some states.

The U.S. doesn't require paid time off for new parents. Instead, it leaves it up to states or employers to provide. In states that do require paid parental leave, an increasing number of fathers are taking time off to care for and bond with their children. In California, men now make up about half of those applying for the leave. Last year, they even surpassed women for the first time since the state started offering the benefit in 2004. Elly Yu of LAist News brings us this report.
UNIDENTIFIED CHILD #1: Give me the ball.

ELLY YU, BYLINE: It's Saturday night, and Karlo Campana is outnumbered. His two young girls take turns shooting a plastic ball into the hoop attached to their bedroom door. Campana goes in for a dunk.
UNIDENTIFIED CHILD #2: Ooh, did it (ph).
CAMPANA: Ooh. Just threw it, and it came back.
YU: On the floor, their baby brother watches in awe from his bouncy chair.
CAMPANA: Want to shoot it, papas? Not yet?

YU: Campana is a dad of three in Orange County, California. He works at an ad agency. And when his son was born this spring, he took paid time off just as he did when his two older daughters were born.
CAMPANA: You need that adjustment. Like, nobody gives you a playbook.
YU: He says having the time off not to think about work or worry about losing income during that time was crucial for him and his family.

CAMPANA: I get to spend time with each of them when they were just, like, in the infant stage, the baby stage, and I get to hold them and, you know, change the poopy diapers, the pee-pee (ph) diapers.

YU: Research shows that paid parental leave benefits the whole family. It's linked to lower infant mortality rates, and paternity leave in particular is linked to better mental and physical health outcomes for moms.

CAMPANA: My wife isn't doing it on her own. I think people don't think about the mental strain. Like, you're - one, you're a little bit sleep-deprived. Like, both parents are involved - mom and dad. It's like, OK, now it's like a team is taking care of this.

YU: California offers up to eight weeks of bonding time for parents after the birth or an adoption of a child. That's on top of six to eight weeks of disability leave moms get to recover after birth. It's one of 14 states and D.C. that have enacted paid bonding leave programs, and more dads are opting in - in California, Colorado, and Washington, sometimes more so than moms.
MOLLY WESTON WILLIAMSON: I think we shouldn't discount the impact of culture change.

YU: Molly Weston Williamson is with the advocacy group Paid Leave for All. When California first started its program two decades ago, men made up fewer than 20% of bonding claim applicants at the time. Now men account for about half.
WILLIAMSON: We're in a very different place in terms of our understanding of gender roles, of paternity leave, of dads' roles than we were 20 plus years ago.

YU: Williamson says there are other factors at play, too, for the growth. California boosted the amount of money workers can get. Now, in that state and in others, it can be as high as 90% of their regular salary.
WILLIAMSON: That makes it a realistic option, and I think we're seeing dads and moms responding to that change.

YU: Still, she says, there's a lot we don't know about the new data about dads. Are more dads than moms working and then filing claims? Are single moms able to access the benefit? One thing that's clear, the growth in these states comes as more parents are feeling strained economically. The American Family Survey out of Brigham Young University found that last year, 7 in 10 Americans said raising children was unaffordable, the biggest single-year jump since the survey started more than a decade ago. Jeremy Pope is a professor at BYU who worked on the survey.

JEREMY POPE: I don't think they want government involved in the decision to have kids, but they worry a lot about how much it costs, and they would like to see ways of making those costs smaller or getting help with those costs.
YU: Back in Orange County, California, Campana juggles between his three kids. His toddler hands the baby the basketball briefly.
YU: At first, Campana wasn't sure he should take paternity leave. His dad worked all the time.
CAMPANA: I felt guilty, for sure. I think dads maybe feel they need to be the provider. They need to be the ones that are only helping their family by bringing money or working.
YU: But he says now he sees he's helping his family by being there. For NPR News, I'm Elly Yu in Los Angeles.

The battle between two of the NFL's most woebegone franchises lived up to its lack of hype Sunday. In fact, in terms of excitement, it more than lived up to it. But the on-field product was a special sort of fun-bad.

Titans 26, Colts 20. It's the first win of the year for Tennessee, and a stunning one at that. The Titans trailed 13-0 at halftime and looked completely lifeless. Bench Cam Ward? Throw in the towel? It seemed on the brink.
And then the Colts, being the generous team they are, quite literally gave it away over the next four possessions:
- Jonathan Taylor fumbled on the first play of the second half. The Titans turned that into a field goal.
- With the Colts in scoring range on the next drive, Daniel Jones threw an atrocious interception. The Titans turned that into another field goal.
- The Colts then went three-and-out and gave up a 58-yard Chimere Dike return, setting up the Titans for their lone offensive touchdown of the day.
- On the next drive, Julius Chestnut blocked a punt, and Oluwafemi Oladejo recovered the loose ball and scored a touchdown.

From up 13-0 to down 20-13 in about 18 minutes of game time. Horrifying stuff. The Colts actually tied the game on a Taylor touchdown, only for the defense to commit an awful pass interference to set up a Titans field goal. Tennessee tacked on another field goal late.
A collapse in all three stages? Against a winless team? For an organization already skating on thin ice? Check, check, check. Which leads me to say ...
Shane Steichen won't last the season, and Chris Ballard and Daniel Jones will be gone between now and Week 1, 2027
Since 2020, there have been 16 in-season coaching changes. Shane Steichen will either be the next or, at the very least, join that list.

This was an unacceptable collapse. The Titans are completely inept offensively. The only way they could do anything was if the Colts blew it, and the Colts blew it over and over again. I've generally been a proponent of Steichen as a good offensive mind, but as a head coach, you have to be more than that. You are responsible for everything, and in that matter, Indianapolis isn't close to good enough.

Steichen can't play the game, though, so we turn to the players ... and the person who chose them. Chris Ballard is in his 10th season as Colts GM. The team has one playoff win over that span, and it was back in 2018, his second year. He has been completely unable to find a quarterback, and his latest attempt is turning out as bad as the others.

Remember, at the start of Ballard's tenure, he had Andrew Luck. Andrew Luck retired ahead of the 2019 season. It's been that long. Inexcusable. He has tried half-measures with veterans. He tried drafting one (Anthony Richardson). He has failed in every measure. The defense remains iffy at best, even after the blockbuster () Sauce Gardner trade.

But really, it all comes back to Jones: He was 22-for-42 for 269 yards, a touchdown and two interceptions. He took six sacks. He's tied for the NFL lead in turnovers. Sunday, he simply did not put an NFL-caliber product on the field.

Remember, the Colts signed him to a two-year, $88 million deal over the offseason, even though they were bidding with ... no one. There is an out after this year that would carry $35 million in dead cap, but continuing with him would be even more punitive for a franchise long overdue for a reset.
Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon is known for and keeping notes. Her only notes needed from Sunday? It's time to clean house.
The Rams won't make the playoffs playing like this
This is simply a non-playoff team right now. Here are the stunning numbers from the Rams' stunning to the Cardinals:
- As a 13.5-point favorite, Matthew Stafford suffered the largest upset of his career. It's also tied for the largest upset in the NFL in the last five years.
- The Rams had zero plays of 20+ yards across their first nine possessions Sunday.

- Stafford's average pass traveled 4.8 yards downfield, the fourth-lowest number of his Rams career and his lowest since 2024. For reference, the lowest air yards per attempt this year is 4.9, belonging to Bo Nix.
- The Rams did not sack Jacoby Brissett and are tied for the third-fewest sacks in the NFL this season.
- The Rams are the fifth preseason Super Bowl favorite in the last 50 years to be under .500 through six games.
- The Rams have won the turnover battle once in six games this season. And they lost that game -- to the Bills last week -- anyway.
Sean McVay summed it up aptly: "There's nothing positive that I can say about today."

The offense has very little juice, outside an occasional excellent play by Puka Nacua or Davante Adams. It just feels really stagnant; Stafford used play action on 37% of his dropbacks last year and averaged 8.4 yards per pass on those throws. This year, it's down to 25% and 7.2, respectively. And when a team doesn't have juice, it has little room for error. But the Rams keep making errors: penalties, turnovers, missed assignments, etc.
Meanwhile, the defense just isn't causing much havoc. And the special teams issues remain. New kicker Blake Grupe got hurt in the first quarter, forcing the Rams to adjust on the fly.
Even if the Rams had won, it's not close to good enough. Sean McVay said as much. If they lose in Week 7, it's officially panic time.
We found an alien lifeform, and his name is Josh Allen
The Browns or Steelers will win the AFC North
Well, well, well, if it isn't a three-way tie atop the AFC North through six weeks?! The Browns, Steelers and Ravens are all 4-2, and the Bengals (on bye this weekend) aren't far behind at 3-2.
Cleveland technically leads the division thanks to Sunday's 13-10 win over Lamar Jackson-less Baltimore, and Pittsburgh is second because it has a better in-division record.

Sorry, Browns and Steelers fans, but neither one of you is winning the division. Cleveland's largest win this season is by four points. It lost to the Jets just last week. Deshaun Watson looked awful Sunday. The Steelers looked similarly awful, needing a late comeback to force overtime against the Baker Mayfield-less Buccaneers. As it turns out, playing against backup quarterbacks is very helpful.

Both teams rank in the bottom half of most major offensive stats. The quarterback play simply isn't good enough and won't be good enough, especially when put up against Lamar Jackson and Joe Burrow rather than Tyler Huntley and Jalon Daniels.
Patriots made a mistake trading for A.J. Brown

A.J. Brown's grand return from IR was ... not so grand. Three catches for 27 yards on 10 targets. Officially, he's been charged with two drops. Unofficially, given his high standards, it was probably more. He even bobbled away a Jets onside kick, but lucky for him, a teammate recovered to clinch the Patriots' 26-19 win.

It's worth being concerned about the debut, but to say the trade is a bust or a mistake would be a drastic overreaction. Yes, it's been a tough start with the injury and the underwhelming return. But let's not write it off. He won on the routes New England brought him in to win: quick in-breakers and deep balls. Drake Maye missed him on one of each, and Brown failed to finish other opportunities he did have. It sounds like a silly thing to say, but if you cut the tape right before the ball arrives, Brown's film would look encouraging.

Of course, he has to make the plays that are there. Getting open doesn't gain yards, score points or win games. Brown will bounce back, and he can still be a huge boost. He came back from his high ankle sprain earlier than expected. Let's give him a week's worth of grace.
C.J. Stroud will be a top-five highest-paid quarterback this offseason ... and deserves it

Another week, another outstanding performance for C.J. Stroud. The fourth-year pro threw for 312 yards, three touchdowns and an interception and led the game-winning drive in the Texans' 34-31 win over the Jaguars.
The numbers are one thing, but the film is just as good, if not better. This is one of the best throws you will see all season.

This is Stroud at his best: laser-accurate, huge arm, can access every part of the field. It's been missed the past few years, and the Texans should be very glad it's back. Not only that, but he is improving at mitigating negative plays. His interception Sunday was really bad, but it was his first all year. He's also taking fewer devastating sacks than he did last season. And he's doing it all while still not having much of a run game.
The Texans and Stroud didn't reach an extension in the offseason. He had been awful in the playoffs, and while both sides said the right things, no agreement happened.

He is very much on the way to earning that massive extension this offseason, though. This offseason is setting up to be a huge one for quarterback deals — Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels, Drake Maye and Bo Nix from the 2024 class, Bryce Young from Stroud's 2023 class and Lamar Jackson are all looking for a new deal. Stroud's deal will put him among the top five highest-paid quarterbacks, and it will be well-deserved.
Brad Idzik will be a hot head-coaching candidate in 2027

The Panthers topped the injury-battered Eagles 25-14 in straightforward fashion. Bryce Young threw a pair of touchdown passes, and Chuba Hubbard ran for 120 yards and a score. Philadelphia was without Jalen Hurts, its top three running backs and a bunch of other players. It's not a super notable result by any measure.
But Philadelphia still has a really good defense, and Brad Idzik flashed excellent play calling, including on both touchdowns to Tommy Tremble.
I was also super impressed by Young's work on RPO throws, something Idzik and Young have worked into this offense really well.

Idzik took over calling plays from Dave Canales this offseason. It has been a perfect promotion. Carolina has one of the most aggressive offenses in the NFL in terms of passing rates. It's a really well-designed offense that empowers Young and accentuates his strengths. In an NFL that loves young, innovative play callers, Idzik is part of the next wave of hotshots.

The players sometimes change. I sat down with four of Benchmark’s partners three years ago, and three of those individuals are no longer with the firm. The capital commitments have changed, too. This summer, Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds, marking only the second time in its 31-year history that it has veered from raising a far smaller vehicle.

But at this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt, the venture firm’s five partners convincingly portrayed a close-knit team that’s not about to put the pedal to the metal, even as many of their rivals do exactly that. The world may be speeding up, but they’re investing at the pace Benchmark always has: just two or three new bets per year per partner. The world is drowning in information, yet their Monday partner meetings still have no agenda. And while economic indicators point to trouble ahead, they don’t seem too bothered, seeing many of the warning signs as products of X-fueled hysteria.

Here’s what Benchmark’s five general partners — gathered together on our stage — had to say at the show. Some of the comments below have been edited for length and clarity; you can watch the full interview at the end of the article.
Benchmark has evolved in some ways, including a bigger core fund and a new growth fund. How do you think about adapting without losing what makes you Benchmark?

Peter Fenton: The craft that hasn’t changed is the core fund: working closely with founders at the beginning. It’s usually a 10-to-15-year commitment, [working] shoulder to shoulder, and that doesn’t scale. There’s also been inflation. We held the core fund at $500 million for 20 years, and it has just inflated to be consistent with the existing economy, which we hadn’t done and that was probably a tactical error on our part.

[As for the growth fund] it’s an expansion of our mandate. In some ways, we get permission from the ecosystem to do more than just the core early-stage business. [Not having this previously] was a fork in our eye. A number of opportunities that came to Benchmark would have returned somewhere between 10 and 1,000x to Benchmark, and we were constricted by our early-stage focus.
Are you thinking to make handful of bets with that $1.25 billion growth fund?

Fenton: We all have different answers, which is the beauty of a partnership. I’d love for us to have, as that great J.P. Morgan paper puts it, the agony and ecstasy of a concentrated portfolio. If the fund is successful, one or two investments will generate 90% of the returns. So I think it’s four to six, maybe seven to eight.
Ev, you joined Benchmark late last year. You’ve worked at Founders Fund, Bond, and Kleiner Perkins. How does Benchmark differ?

Ev Randall: Every firm is ultimately a collection of the people within the firm and how they work together. Some are very hierarchical, with a 50- or 60-person investment team and investment processes that are federated into product groups. And then you have small partnerships. Very early in my career, I was drawn to small partnerships because they allow a higher level of throughput and fidelity in your conversations, where you don’t feel like you’re making decisions through some Byzantine corporate structure. You’re going out on the field together, like a sports team.

And then the other piece is: You have to find your people, You have to find people who you not only like but admire. With Benchmark, with the current crop of GPs, it was obvious that everyone liked each other and got along, but it went deeper than that. It’s a group that admires each other and learns from each other. That mix of attributes is very rare, and when I saw it, I immediately wanted to join, and I think Jack felt the same way also as a newcomer.

Jack, you joined in February, but it was just a year ago that you raised a second, $275 million fund for your own firm in what you told the Wall Street Journal took one week. You have a hugely popular podcast. Why join Benchmark?

Jack Altman: It’s funny. I did the podcast with these guys at the start of this year, and during that podcast, obviously we talked about the commitment to being a small fund, but more than that, what I heard was that they want to be the first people who founders call, they want to be concentrated, and they just care. So much in this industry gets tied up in money and status, and what I felt from the Benchmark team then, and ten times more as I’ve gotten to know them so well, is it’s a group that really cares about founders and helping companies. And I did enjoy being an individual investor. . .but in a market this crazy, I don’t know how I’d feel, figuring it out on my own. Having a group of people who are so smart and focused and driven to learn it with and from has been awesome. There’s no better place to learn.
I’m told you meet on Mondays with no agenda.
Chethan Puttagunta: Jack tried to make an agenda. [Laughs.]
Altman: I’ve got an agenda for next Monday.

Eric Vishria: It’s weirdly arbitrary, honestly. It’s an ongoing conversation. In a time of rapid change, you’re trying to figure out what’s becoming possible that wasn’t possible six months ago, and who’s bending light. We talk about what companies we’re meeting, what piqued our interest and why, what we’re seeing in board meetings. You can try to systematize it, but one of the beauties of five people is you don’t have to. It’s a decades-long conversation that only works if you’re small and actually enjoy spending time together. After this session, we’re having dinner with one of the very few entrepreneurs who has built a multi-hundred-billion-dollar company, someone we’re not invested in, just to stretch our thinking.
Puttagunta: Part of not having an agenda is you need space to be reactive. If a founder needs help landing an executive or a strategic partnership, the five of us can be at their disposal.
You’re an equal partnership. Can one person put the kibosh on a deal?
Puttagunta: Nobody knows. We don’t have rules around it.
Altman: I actually don’t know. I was waiting to see what someone else [said].

Altman: Because the firm is structured around a low volume of deals, you don’t actually want to have all of this rigor. If we invested in 100 or 200 companies a year, you’d want a CRM and a formal voting process. Because it’s so rare, the lack of structure is a huge asset.

Fenton: One of the differentiating aspects of our brand is we’re not so cocksure to come in and say ‘winner’ or ‘loser.’ It’s not Shark Tank. We sort of feel awe, for lack of a better term, at all the possibilities . . . The occasional case where someone comes in who’s polarizing — the entrepreneurs feel that. If someone in the room doesn’t like you, we’re not a great partner.
Companies are growing faster than ever. I’d think it’s easier to feel you’re missing out on opportunities if you don’t invest with greater frequency. Have you picked up the pace?

Puttagunta: I think the pace is consistent. I think part of the reality of venture capital in our business is that we are not going to be part of every successful company, and that’s okay. There are companies that we identify, we find that the entrepreneur has some great strength, and we want to amplify that strength. And it’s our job to find a way to work with that person. It kind of doesn’t matter how much capital they want to raise, or what structure, or where they are. You just have to work through all that stuff.

One thing that founders are interested in as a trend is VCs backing competing companies. Has that VC-founder pact changed because companies are growing so quickly and expanding into one another’s territory?

Vishria: One of the things we have an ethos around is, we are making a commitment to an entrepreneur, and through that commitment, we’re saying we’re going to work with you in this thing, and whatever that thing is, and we are working closely enough where it matters, and it should matter to them, and as it matters to us. The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly, and so you do have companies that will naturally evolve from one thing to another, or pivot or change, and you are going to get conflicts. That’s just the reality of the of the kind of current dynamic. . .

Of course, we’re maintaining confidentiality and doing those things and fortunate to not end up in in that type of insane direct conflict [as happened recently with rival companies Factory and Cognition]. . . that commitment of exclusivity in that area is really important. But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.

Puttagunta: And I think people are ultra ambitious in this AI era. As the cost of coding new products effectively goes to zero, founders see a surface area and they want to attack the surface area, and so I think it’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other. But there’s a way to be there’s a way to maintain that relationship and be respectful.
Jack, have you made an investment for Benchmark yet, and if so, did you feel a lot of pressure with that first deal?

Altman: I have, a few, and some are recent, so not all are disclosed. My background was software, but since joining, I’ve done chips, robotics and infra. Someone asked me when I joined, ‘How was the onboarding?’ And I was like, ‘It was perfect. There was no onboarding.’ Either Chethan or Eric told me early on, ‘Hey, you’re going to feel tight on your first one. Don’t. You’re going to make many investments while you’re here. This whole game includes crazy power laws. The odds of it being your first are low.’ . . . I trusted they understood what my shape was as a person, as an investor, and I was going to just try to stay as consistent to that as I could.

It really is a group dynamic on a lot of these. The investments I’ve made, I don’t think we would have won them if I didn’t have my partners. I don’t know that I would have been able to know how to get to a yes without them.
Eric, the AI chip company Cerebras was an unusual bet for Benchmark at the time it was made. What persuaded you to move forward with it?

Vishria: We invested in the spring of 2016, in the first round. We hadn’t made a hardware investment in 10 years. The founders seemed good, they had a very simple thesis, and I didn’t understand most of the rest. On the Sunday night before they came back to pitch the partnership, Peter told me it went against everything he’d learned in venture. Then, after the Monday pitch, he had flipped. A big part of it is understanding each other’s instincts. That began a journey of lots of ups and downs and many potential deaths of the company along the way, and it’s far from over. The romanticism of falling in love with a founder and an idea is why we do this.

Fenton: Andrew and his co-founders are heretics. What they were saying was unorthodox, and you see it today, with people dumping on the stock because it’s polarizing. That’s exactly where we have to be as investors. If it’s consensus, why is there a startup?

The Army officially inactivated the 8th Psychological Operations Group (Airborne) in a ceremony at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, on Sept. 29.

“I could not be prouder of the men and women that stand before us today and those that came before us to inactivate the unit,” Col. Robert Cusick, the group’s commanding officer, said. “8th PSYOP Group introduced new concepts that will remain for years to come.”

8th POG, nicknamed the “Phantom Knights,” was formally activated on Nov. 16, 2013, after operating provisionally for two years. It was one of four Army PSYOP groups, including the active-duty 4th Psychological Operations Group (Airborne) and the Army Reserve’s 2nd and 7th Psychological Operations Groups.

The term “inactivation” signifies that the group is being decommissioned for an indeterminate period during some form of restructuring and reorganization — not necessarily that it is being deactivated or dissolved.

The 8th POG included the 3rd PSYOP Battalion (Airborne) and the 9th PSYOP Battalion (Airborne). The 3rd POB influences print, radio and broadcast information operations around the world, while the 9th POB is typically involved in operations like dropping leaflets and cultivating local communities where Special Forces may be operating.
The Information Warfare Center, organized in 2020, was also under the aegis of the 8th PG. The IWC combines intelligence operations and information warfare specifically for Army Special Forces.

The inactivation comes just two months after the Army activated Delta Company, 7th Psychological Operations Battalion. The 7th was previously assigned to the 4th Psychological Operations Group (Airborne) but is now under the 3rd Special Forces Group (Airborne). That group is focused on psychological operations primarily under U.S. Africa Command’s purview.

Some military officials and analysts have argued that the U.S. needs to overhaul its approach to psychological operations and information warfare groups — hence the Delta Company activation and the retirement of the 8th POG.

“What is most concerning is not simply that adversaries invest in information warfare, but that they can often employ it faster and more coherently than we can respond,” Maj. Ryan Walters, an active-duty U.S. Army Psychological Operations officer, wrote in Small Wars Journal in January. “In practice, adversaries win by compressing the time between sensing, shaping, and exploiting, while U.S. forces remain constrained by approval latency, fragmented execution, and inconsistent assessment. The result is a temporal mismatch in which effects arrive after decisions are already made.”

U.S. defense firm Anduril could eventually manufacture its newly unveiled Steelfin interceptor missiles in Europe, a company executive said this week, as governments aim to expand air defense production after global conflicts highlighted shortages of interceptor missiles.

“I certainly hope that something like Steelfin could become a capability that we engage with both the Polish customer and industry,” Brian Moran, Anduril’s vice president for Europe, told Reuters on Monday.
“We would definitely consider engaging European partners and customers on this capability.” Steelfin is due to undergo flight testing in 2027, according to Anduril.
Wars in Ukraine and the Gulf have strained stocks of air defense interceptor missiles and caused delivery delays.
Moran said Anduril saw Steelfin as a complementary system that could provide a more affordable interceptor alongside existing missile defense systems like the Patriot and others.
The company is already in talks to establish production in Poland of its Barracuda-500 cruise missile, and Moran said that experience could open the door to additional manufacturing projects.

“We’re having a very good experience with our industry partner here, PGZ,” he said, adding that discussions were also under way with the defense ministry and other government agencies. PGZ is Poland’s state-owned arms group.
Poland, one of NATO’s top defense spenders relative to the size of its economy, is seeking to expand domestic arms production and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers.
Moran said talks with PGZ, its WZL-2 unit and the government were focused on balancing local production with delivery speed and Poland’s specific military requirements.

Asked about growing calls in Europe for defense industrial sovereignty, Moran said the term could mean different things, from security of supply and maintenance capabilities to control over software upgrades and future modifications.

“Sovereignty has a cost. There’s a cost to localization. There’s cost in terms of timing and just schedule. And those need to be considered in light of the threats that Europe collectively is facing.”

While governments also want economic benefits from defense spending, the military outcome is most important, he said, adding that greater localization can come with additional costs and longer timelines.
